tldr: The authors propose FAMOS, a framework that predicts movable-part segmentation and joint parameters in a single feed-forward pass from just a few sparse partial point clouds. Using a loss focused on observed articulation range and procedural data generation, it generalizes robustly even to unseen objects.
hero_caption: Overall framework of FAMOS. Partial point clouds from different states and viewpoints are tokenized and processed jointly with part queries via the Multi-state Articulation Transformer to predict part segmentation, joint types, and parameters all at once.
overview:
For robots to operate in human environments—such as opening refrigerator doors or pulling out drawers—they need to accurately understand an object's "articulation": where and how its parts move. However, conventional optimization-based methods take minutes of compute and require dense multi-view images. Meanwhile, recent fast feed-forward deep learning models infer articulation from a single image or point cloud by relying on category-level shape priors, which often leads to incorrect joint orientations on unseen object shapes.

To address this, the authors developed FAMOS, a new feed-forward approach that directly estimates joint parameters and movable parts from a sparse, unordered set of partial point clouds by leveraging actual motion cues. At its core are a Transformer architecture with alternating state-wise and global attention, and an "observed articulation span" objective that supervises the range of motion exhibited across the inputs. This prevents the model from relying on single-view guesswork and encourages it to capture geometric changes across multiple states.

Additionally, to tackle the scarcity of 3D articulated object data, the authors built a procedural pipeline that autonomously generates an infinite stream of assets from geometric primitives. Evaluated on standard benchmarks such as PartNet-Mobility, FAMOS significantly outperforms existing feed-forward baselines and matches or exceeds optimization-based methods while running roughly 3,000 times faster (~0.1 seconds).
contributions: Proposed FAMOS, a novel model that predicts movable-part segmentation and joint parameters from a sparse, unordered set of partial point clouds in a single feed-forward pass.

Introduced the Multi-state Articulation Transformer, which balances within-state geometric context and cross-state correspondences, along with an observed articulation span objective that forces the model to leverage multiple states.
Developed a procedural generator that synthesizes self-annotated models on the fly during training from geometric primitives, overcoming the shortage of articulated object training data.
Demonstrated substantial accuracy improvements over prior methods across three benchmarks and casual real-world captures, achieving a ~3,000x inference speedup.

sections.heading: How to Model Moving Objects: Shifting from Appearance Guesswork to Observing Motion
sections.summary: Operating articulated objects in home environments requires estimating motion directions and joint axes. However, existing work is either computationally heavy or over-relies on appearance priors and fails on unseen shapes. FAMOS breaks through this barrier by capturing actual motion from a few partial observations to instantly derive articulation.
sections.details:
Everyday environments are full of articulated objects like doors, drawers, and scissors. For robots to manipulate them, they must understand in 3D which parts move and how.

Yet, existing approaches face significant limitations. Test-time optimization methods based on NeRF or 3D Gaussian Splatting require dozens of dense multi-view images per state and take minutes to tens of minutes per object. Video-based tracking methods tend to accumulate tracking drift due to occlusions and simultaneous multi-part motion. On the other hand, feed-forward methods are fast, but most predict articulation from only a single static state, effectively memorizing the average shape of training categories and guessing. They struggle when faced with novel shapes or incomplete inputs.

FAMOS addresses this by taking a few sparse, unordered partial point clouds—such as those casually captured in daily life—and estimating articulation based on the motion actually observed. Key to this approach are a Transformer architecture that allows direct point-to-point interactions across different states and a novel training objective that predicts the angle or translation span across the input set. Furthermore, by introducing a procedural generation pipeline to solve the severe shortage of 3D articulated datasets, the authors substantially boost the model's generalization capability.

sections.heading: From Dense Scans and Video Tracking to Feed-Forward Prediction
sections.summary: Articulation modeling has evolved from dense multi-view optimization and video tracking to single-input feed-forward prediction. FAMOS combines the strengths of these approaches while uniquely handling unordered, multi-state partial point clouds.
sections.details:
### Reconstruction from Dense Multi-View Inputs
Historically, the dominant approach has been to capture dense camera views for each of two articulated states and optimize per-instance neural implicit representations or 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). While this yields high-quality reconstructions, the computational cost is extremely heavy and often requires prior knowledge of the number of movable parts, limiting real-world scalability.

### Articulation Modeling from Manipulation Videos
Methods estimating articulation from sequential 4D point clouds or videos have also been proposed. However, chaining point tracking modules often causes tracking errors to accumulate due to occlusions and part overlaps. They also assume continuous temporal video frames.

### Feed-Forward Methods
Recently, fast models predicting articulation directly from a single mesh or point cloud have emerged. However, single-state approaches must infer articulation purely from static geometric features, making them vulnerable to shape variations. While some prior works accept multiple states (such as Ditto or ART), they impose rigid constraints, such as requiring complete point clouds or fixing the number of parts and states. FAMOS handles a variable number of partial point cloud inputs in a single forward pass without pre-specifying part counts.

sections.heading: Network Design via Cross-State Attention and Articulation Span
sections.summary: Partial point clouds are tokenized with a pretrained backbone and passed into a Transformer with alternating state-wise and global attention. An auxiliary loss predicting the motion span across states encourages the network to fully leverage multi-state cues.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation
The input is a set of $S$ sparse partial point clouds $\mathcal{X} = \{\mathbf{X}_s\}_{s=1}^S$ obtained from different articulation states and viewpoints. The number of states $S$ is variable and supports $S=1$ (single view). The outputs are: (1) the total number of parts $P$ including the static base and movable parts, (2) per-point part assignment labels (segmentation), and (3) joint parameters for each part (rotation axis and origin, or translation direction).

### 3.2 Multi-State Articulation Transformer
Point clouds are tokenized using a frozen PartField backbone combined with coordinate and normal embeddings. Crucially, tokens are not assigned a state index, allowing the model to flexibly handle any number of input states.

The model maintains $K$ learnable part queries and repeats two alternating attention stages across $L$ layers:
- **State-wise Attention**: Self-attention is performed among point tokens within the same observation (state) to aggregate local geometric context. Concurrently, part queries attend to each other to coordinate their roles.
- **Global Attention**: Point tokens from all states and part queries are concatenated and attended to jointly. This is the key design: direct point-to-point communication without query bottlenecks enables the model to capture geometric correspondences across views and occluded areas.

### 3.3 Observed Articulation Span
Because joint axes and origins are intrinsic properties of an object, plausible values can often be predicted from static appearance alone. Consequently, supervising only with joint parameters creates a learning shortcut where the model ignores multi-state inputs and relies on memorization from a single view.
To prevent this, the authors introduce an auxiliary task: predicting the observed articulation span $\Delta_p = \max_{s \in \mathcal{V}_p} \theta_{s,p} - \min_{s \in \mathcal{V}_p} \theta_{s,p}$, representing the maximum angle or translation distance the part moves across the input observations. Because this span cannot be predicted without inspecting the entire observation set and tracking parts across states, it strongly encourages the model to integrate multi-state information.

### 3.5 Procedural Data Generation
To address the shortage of articulated 3D training data, the authors built a system that procedurally generates 15 families of objects (e.g., cabinets, appliances) by assembling geometric primitives like boxes and cylinders. By randomly varying dimensions and part counts, new shapes with perfect ground-truth annotations are generated in real time on the CPU during training.

sections.heading: High Accuracy on Unseen Objects: ~3,000x Speedup and Real-World Generalization
sections.summary: FAMOS was evaluated on three datasets: PartNet-Mobility, ACD, and ArtiCraft-10K. It outperforms both feed-forward and optimization-based baselines with an inference latency of just 0.1 seconds. Despite training only on synthetic data, it generalizes well to real-world captures.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Baselines
Evaluations were conducted on PartNet-Mobility (in-distribution), ACD (unseen geometry and complex structures), and ArtiCraft-10K (generated automatically by LLM agents). Baselines include a multi-input extension of the representative feed-forward model Particulate, as well as recent optimization methods ReArt (4D point clouds) and ArtGS (3DGS).

### Quantitative Results
In part segmentation (Table 1), FAMOS achieves the top scores across all benchmarks. Notably, on the unseen ACD dataset, it outperforms Particulate by 28.2 points in F1 score. Optimization baselines remain below 60% F1 despite receiving dense inputs.
For joint estimation (Table 2), under the strictest metric (MAO, requiring joint type match, axis error < 5°, and origin error < 5%), FAMOS achieves decisive scores: 98.4 on PartNet-Mobility, 64.5 on ACD, and 90.0 on ArtiCraft. It detects substantially more parts correctly than baselines while maintaining low geometric error.

### Ablations and Analysis
Ablation studies (Table 4) show that replacing Global Attention with indirect register token communication drops MAO on ACD by 8.1 points, and removing the observed articulation span loss drops it by 5.7 points. These numbers confirm the importance of direct point attention and motion span supervision.
Experiments on the number of input states (Figure 7(b)) show a sharp performance gain when increasing from 1 to 2 states, confirming that observed motion provides critical cues for articulation estimation.

### Runtime and Real-World Data
While optimization-based ReArt takes 182 seconds and ArtGS takes 297 seconds per object, FAMOS completes inference in just 0.1 seconds (~3,000x faster). Furthermore, when fed casual smartphone photos of real-world furniture processed through SAM2 and a point cloud reconstructor, FAMOS accurately predicts parts and revolution/prismatic axes.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook
sections.summary: FAMOS achieves fast, accurate articulation modeling from sparse partial point clouds. Combining a cross-state Transformer architecture, an observed articulation span loss, and procedural data generation allows it to overcome previous limitations.
sections.details:
This work presents FAMOS, a feed-forward model that reconstructs articulated objects from a few incomplete observations. Through the Multi-state Articulation Transformer with state-wise and global attention and a novel objective supervising observed motion range, the model moves away from shape guessing and accurately predicts joint parameters based on observed motion.

In addition, the procedural asset generator directly addresses the core bottleneck of articulated data scarcity. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over both optimization-based and feed-forward baselines, along with successful execution on real-world data. Fast and robust articulation perception offers a strong foundation for robotic manipulation and dynamic real-world interaction.

sections.heading: Appendix: Computational Cost and Real-World Details
sections.summary: The appendix provides scalability analyses with respect to input token counts, highlights procedural generation speed, and details additional real-world qualitative results and current limitations.
sections.details:
### Computational Complexity and Scalability
While Global Attention scales quadratically with point and state counts, FlashAttention keeps it very lightweight in practice. In the default setting ($S=2$ states, $N=2048$ points), GPU memory usage is only 1.56 GiB with a latency of 65.6 ms. Even under a stress test with 12 states and 8,192 points (~98k tokens total), it runs in 1.20 seconds using 10.66 GiB, demonstrating solid scalability to larger observation sets.

### Procedural Generation Efficiency
The on-the-fly generation pipeline produces approximately 334 assets per second per CPU process (~3 ms per asset), ensuring it never bottlenecks training. Its key strength is delivering a continuous stream of diverse data without manual annotation.

### Limitations and Failure Modes
Current limitations remain. First, performance degrades on shapes far outside the training distribution. Second, movable parts that are very small relative to the object (such as handles or small switches) are difficult to segment due to point cloud resolution limits. Third, the model is currently restricted to depth-1 kinematic trees where movable parts attach directly to a static base; it cannot handle multi-link kinematic chains like multi-joint robotic arms.

captions.F9: Additional predictions on casual real-world captures. Accurate part segmentations and joint axes are recovered from noisy, incomplete point clouds of everyday items like books and cabinets.

takeaways: Directly comparing cross-state changes (motion) across even a few coarse point clouds provides far better generalization than guessing articulation from single-view appearance.
Auxiliary tasks supervising cross-state variation—such as the observed articulation span loss—are highly effective at preventing models from taking shortcuts and ignoring multi-state inputs.
Procedural generation using simple geometric primitives offers a practical, on-the-fly pretraining solution to the shortage of 3D articulated datasets.
Running in just 0.1 seconds (~3,000x faster than optimization methods) makes FAMOS easy to integrate into real-time robot interaction planning.
limitations: Restricted to depth-1 kinematic trees where parts attach directly to a static base; cannot handle multi-link kinematic chains like robot arms.
Prone to segmentation failures when parts are very small relative to the whole object (knobs, keys, small buttons) or when point clouds suffer from heavy noise and missing regions.
While procedural generation expands diversity, category coverage remains limited compared to massive general-purpose 3D shape datasets.
